source_review.notes: Checked the official NIST SP 800-145 and SP 800-144 records, CISA Cloud Security Technical Reference Architecture, CSA CCM 4.1 and its 2026 introductory guidance, current AWS and Microsoft responsibility documentation, Microsoft reliability guidance, Google shared-responsibility/shared-fate guidance, and the AICPA SOC overview. Provider formulations are presented as examples rather than universal allocations; claims retain service, contract, date, configuration, and assurance-scope boundaries.

evidence: Checked actor set A, obligation set O, exact-service set S, resource set R, scope, source, performer, accountable-owner, interface, evidence, and escalation notation for definition before use.
Checked set membership and non-empty predicates in the structural coverage expression.
Confirmed that exactly-one accountability is labeled an operating invariant rather than a theorem.
notation_and_syntax.notes: The notation is intentionally lightweight and does not claim that organizational adequacy reduces to set membership.

evidence: Recomputed four synthetic obligation records.
Confirmed IAM-01, REC-01, and LOG-01 each have non-empty accountable, performers, evidence, and escalation fields.
Confirmed COST-01 lacks accountable owner, evidence, and escalation, yielding three complete records and one gap.
Confirmed three records contain provider plus at least one other performer.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The deterministic output exactly matches the snippet report; counts do not measure real control effectiveness.

evidence: Re-derived covered(o) as requiring performer, accountable owner, interface, evidence, and escalation for every applicable obligation.
Checked that moving a mechanism to a provider does not entail transfer of customer mission, legal, continuity, or risk-acceptance accountability.
Checked that splitting two distinct decisions into two obligations preserves the one-accountable-owner invariant.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: Structural coverage is necessary but explicitly not sufficient for secure, reliable, private, compliant, or economical operation.

evidence: Reviewed IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, private, hybrid, multi-provider, managed database, serverless, and SaaS responsibility shifts.
Reviewed gaps at IAM, log-delivery, backup/restore, encryption, incident-support, deprecation, endpoint, subprocessor, deletion, and exit boundaries.

Reviewed stale assurance, out-of-scope services and regions, complementary controls, subservice carve-outs, expired evidence, conflicting owners, absent escalation, and provider-feature-not-enabled cases.
Reviewed hospital clinical-data and municipal benefits-data transfers for legal, privacy, safety, fairness, accessibility, records, and executive authority.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: High-consequence examples require actual named authorized humans and make no external-review claim.

evidence: Traced exact service scope, one accountable customer authority, explicit performers, complementary shared verbs, interfaces, evidence, escalation, and review triggers through exposition, examples, and answers.
Confirmed provider capability is never equated with customer enablement or successful use.
Confirmed provider assurance is bounded by service, region, control, period, exceptions, prerequisites, and customer configuration.
Confirmed security, privacy, reliability, operations, economics, incidents, lifecycle, and exit all receive explicit treatment.
invariant_checking.notes: Every completion claim remains conditional on obligation discovery and current evidence.

evidence: Reviewed counterexamples in which every component behaves as documented but the combined system fails because no actor owns audit export, restore testing, or a boundary handoff.
Reviewed why certification of a provider-scoped subject cannot entail compliance of a customer workload.
Reviewed why an availability SLA cannot entail a workload RTO or RPO.
Reviewed the explicit falsification rule: an unowned restore, inaccessible log, expired report, or undocumented subprocessor defeats a completeness claim.
proof_review.notes: The chapter offers trace arguments and counterexamples, not a universal proof that a responsibility register is exhaustive.

evidence: Audited uses of proof, establish, guarantee, covered, compliant, complete, adequate, inherited, shared, and accountable.
Confirmed that the completeness argument is explicitly called a reviewable trace rather than mathematical proof.
Confirmed that one-accountable-owner is identified as an operating invariant and that assignments can change with exact services and contracts.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: No diagram, register, structural check, feature, SLA, certification, or internal review is elevated to universal proof.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/CLOUD-002/report.json records deterministic local execution for cloud-responsibility-register-check.
The chapter explicitly limits the run to non-emptiness and count behavior over four synthetic records.
Provider documentation and assurance artifacts are described as scoped evidence whose freshness, provenance, independence, completeness, and relevance require review.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No real workload security, privacy, reliability, compliance, cost, recovery, provider performance, legal approval, safety approval, or external review is claimed.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed responsibility, accountability, objective, implementation, inheritance, assurance, attestation, certification, compliance, residual risk, boundary control, RACI, SLA, SLO, provider, customer, internal provider, performer, evidence producer, and decision authority as distinct concepts.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed exact-service inventory, obligation derivation, provider document and contract inspection, responsibility assignment, interface mapping, evidence paths, assurance-scope review, gap and overlap analysis, incident coordination, recovery exercises, deprecation response, and lifecycle review. Internal cloud-engineering-practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from first principles through service-model shifts, obligation registers, security/privacy/reliability/operations/economics, evidence, assurance, change, and incident response. Ten distinct worked examples and five complete exercises progress from definition through derivation, diagnosis, design comparison, and unfamiliar high-consequence transfer.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external academic, cloud-provider, cloud-customer, security, reliability, privacy, legal, clinical-safety, public-benefits, accessibility, procurement, audit, regulatory, certification, or practitioner review is claimed.
